https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/22/at-l.text: Typhoon Dujuan left at least four people dead and 22 injured in Japan, while thousands of houses near Tokyo were without power after the storm swept through the region, authorities said on Tuesday.Officials warned that the death toll may continue to rise as six people remain missing, noting that search and rescue operations were underway to locate them.The typhoon moved away from Japan's coast and out into the Pacific by the morning, allowing authorities to lift or downgrade most heavy rain and landslide warnings.Dujuan had already led to the early closure in the capital of one of the world's biggest video game trade fairs.Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn, with other storms this season disrupting some events at the Asian Games being held in the country.The Fire and Disaster Management Agency said three people died in Chiba prefecture and one in Kanagawa region, both near the capital, Tokyo.Entire areas were completely submerged by floodwaters, causing considerable damage and bringing many critical services, major roads and public transportation to a standstill.More than 45,000 households in Chiba near Tokyo were still without electricity on Tuesday afternoon, while over 460 houses suffered varying degrees of damage.Although Dujuan weakened as it moved northeast, it dumped record rainfall in parts of the Tokyo area.Oshima, an island about 120 kilometres south of central Tokyo, recorded 832 millimetres of rain over a 48-hour period, more than double its average rainfall for the whole of September, public broadcaster NHK reported.Rainfall in Tokyo's Edogawa Ward reached a record 282.5 millimetres over 24 hours.Scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the risk posed by heavy rains because a warmer atmosphere holds more water.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text: Islanders and volunteers have been digging in the early medieval cemetery, where they have discovered the earlier buildings, burial grounds and other finds. Photograph: Robert Hay View image in fullscreen Islanders and volunteers have been digging in the early medieval cemetery, where they have discovered the earlier buildings, burial grounds and other finds. Photograph: Robert Hay Archaeology ‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of Christianity Community-funded archaeological excavations of ‘really important’ sixth-century monastery also rewrite story of Lismore Esther Addley Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island. This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity . But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history. A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology , to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral. View image in fullscreen The site contains extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings. Photograph: Robert Hay Their “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west. In addition, the excavations uncovered rare evidence of slightly later high-status craftworking, including huge numbers of crucibles which had been used to cast gold and silver. The finds have shown that rather than being a small island church in an overlooked backwater, the monastery of Lios Mór, founded by Saint Mo Luóc or Moluag , was a high-ranking site of international importance, experts say. To Robert Hay, a retired plant scientist who moved to the island in 2001 and who coordinated the fundraising and volunteer efforts, the experience was thrilling. “We were [excavating] in this really unfavourable, boggy area. To be digging out the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland – it’s extraordinary,” he said. View image in fullscreen A crucible freshly out of the soil. Photograph: Robert Hay “The most exciting moment for me was when they were doing the post-excavation analysis and they found that they had been melting gold, copper, silver, and they were making jewellery on our little island in the seventh century.” While plenty of islanders have an idle interest in its history, a “dynamic minority” of mostly older people had mustered the volunteers and funds to carry out the digs, said Hay. Raising the low five-figure sum needed to pay for it all had been “just a business of getting down to it and organising and so on”, he said. “It was actually a lot easier than what my previous job used to be.” Gordon Noble, a professor of archaeology at the University of Aberdeen, said the finds were highly significant. “We know about sites like Iona having these very famous monastic sites from this early medieval world. But apart from the association with Moluag and a piece of sculpture from this site, we knew practically nothing really about Lismore. So it was hugely exciting to see the results emerging through the local group’s work with Clare [Ellis] … This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment.” View image in fullscreen Newly identified early-medieval sculpture fragments from Lios Mòr. Photograph: Gordon Noble While professional archaeologists often worked with local people, Noble said, “it’s not always the community themselves coming up with the ideas. Here, it was very much a bottom-up approach of the heritage society coming up with a plan, working with professionals – and lo and behold, what a great series of discoveries they’ve made at the site.” Hay said he hoped the finds would go some way to restoring the reputation of Moluag, who has long been overshadowed by the more celebrated Saint Columba, the founder of Iona and the subject of an influential ninth-century biography. “Unfortunately, Moluag never had a hagiographer, so his contribution to the evangelisation of Scotland has been very much underestimated,” he said. “So finding his monastic site and [the evidence of metalworking] – it’s all about recalibrating the situation. I think Moluag had a very big impact on the evangelising of Scotland, but unfortunately, he didn’t get his PR right.” The results of the community excavations will be published in the forthcoming edition of Antiquity . https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d.text: Image source, Getty Images Published 7 hours ago At least three people have been killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday. Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped. Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries. The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause. Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening. Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning. "All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said. Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP. Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz. "When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said. The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities. On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.
